profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a large pediatric outpatient network after the first month of a sinusitis antibiotic stewardship dashboard showed an unexpected pattern: clinics that continued prescribing more amoxicillin-clavulanate did not appear to have worse 'treatment failure' rates than clinics using more amoxicillin, but parent callbacks for diarrhea and candidiasis seemed higher. The team is trying to diagnose why the local dashboard does not line up cleanly with the recently circulated national cohort study on pediatric acute sinusitis, and to decide what should be adjusted first: the measure logic, the clinical decision support exclusions, or the rollout message to frontline clinicians. The agenda is to review the signal, compare it to the study design, identify likely root causes for the discrepancy, and agree on a practical next step for the next reporting cycle. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for refining the local review process and stewardship intervention.

members.name: Dr. Elena Ramirez
members.expertise: General pediatrics, outpatient acute respiratory infections, clinical workflow in urgent care and telehealth
members.background: Elena oversees antibiotic prescribing quality across six pediatric urgent care sites and previously led a parent-callback initiative focused on return visits after respiratory infections.
members.private_state: She wants a practical explanation she can give frontline clinicians quickly, prefers not to burden visits with more exceptions, and is worried the dashboard may make clinicians distrust stewardship recommendations if the numbers feel disconnected from what they see in follow-up calls.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'treatment failure' in outpatient sinusitis, they naturally include the clinically meaningful events her teams see most often: parent calls, portal messages, and antibiotic changes after reassessment, not just claims-visible acute care utilization.
The relevant patient pool for troubleshooting is the urgent care sinusitis population she supervises, because that is where the prescribing push happened and where staff feedback is coming from.
If a case is described as 'uncomplicated sinusitis,' routine outpatient prescribing exceptions are narrow and mostly limited to obvious factors like penicillin allergy or known chronic sinus disease.
A 'same-day prescription' effectively means the clinician selected and sent an antibiotic at the index visit, regardless of whether the family picked it up that evening or the next day.

members.name: Priya Shah, PharmD
members.role: Ambulatory Antimicrobial Stewardship Pharmacist and Quality Informatics Lead
members.expertise: Pediatric antibiotic stewardship, EHR measure logic, pharmacy claims interpretation, CDS implementation
members.background: Priya built the network's sinusitis prescribing dashboard using a combination of encounter data, fill data, and inherited decision-support logic adapted from prior respiratory stewardship work.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the credibility of the reporting infrastructure, avoid ad hoc metric changes that break month-to-month comparability, and keep the intervention aligned with publishable definitions and payer-facing quality methods.
hidden_assumptions: When the group says 'treatment failure,' they mean the study-style composite tied to measurable downstream utilization or a new antibiotic dispensation within 1 to 14 days, not phone-based symptom management.

A discussion of the sinusitis prescribing problem defaults to the network-level outpatient denominator, including urgent care, primary care, and telehealth, because the dashboard was designed for system reporting rather than one service line.

The term 'uncomplicated' already inherits the broader exclusion rules embedded in the CDS build, including recent antibiotic exposure, conjunctivitis or otitis co-diagnosis, and other flags carried over from prior stewardship logic.

A 'same-day prescription' is only analytically valid if the medication was actually dispensed on the same calendar day as the index encounter, because that is how the cohort was constructed and how exposure certainty is maintained.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the clinic's 'failure rate' and compare it with the published study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any clinically meaningful deterioration or unresolved case leading to parent outreach, a reassessment, or a switched antibiotic within about two weeks, including phone and portal follow-up managed outside the ED.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the study-like composite: new antibiotic dispensation, ED or inpatient encounter for sinusitis, or inpatient sinusitis complication in days 1 to 14.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both definitions sound standard in a stewardship conversation, and both members are sincerely using the same phrase in a quality-improvement context; neither expects the other to mean something radically different because 'failure rate' is treated as already-established vocabulary.

misalignment_points.topic: Which sinusitis population they are troubleshooting
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'our sinusitis cases' and 'the revisit numbers from last month.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking specifically about urgent care index visits, because those clinicians received the prescribing push and generated the complaints about side effects and callbacks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking about the full outpatient dashboard denominator, which includes urgent care, pediatric primary care, and telehealth encounters coded as acute sinusitis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same organization and month are being discussed, so the reference feels shared; because urgent care contributes a large fraction of cases, the aggregate patterns are similar enough that the difference in denominator does not immediately stand out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the recommendation applies to 'uncomplicated sinusitis' and talk about narrowing clavulanate use there.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'uncomplicated' excludes only obvious major exceptions such as penicillin allergy, immunocompromise, and chronic sinus disease, leaving most routine sinusitis visits in scope.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'uncomplicated' already excludes a broader inherited set in the CDS and dashboard logic, including recent antibiotic exposure, concurrent otitis or conjunctivitis, and other features that automatically keep amoxicillin-clavulanate acceptable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both view their definition as routine background clinical logic, so the phrase feels self-explanatory; because the broader exclusions were embedded in a prior build rather than newly debated, M2 does not think to restate them and M1 assumes the wording is plain-language clinical rather than technical logic.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention reviewing 'same-day prescriptions' to align with the study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means antibiotics electronically prescribed during the index visit, even if families fill them the next morning after discussing symptoms at home.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means medications actually dispensed on the same calendar day as the encounter, because the measure uses fill data to define exposure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinical conversation, 'prescription' usually refers to the clinician's action, while in pharmacy analytics it often means a completed dispensation; both usages are common and contextually reasonable, so surface agreement feels natural.

turns.inner_thought: What is bothering me is the disconnect between what urgent care teams are living and what the dashboard says. In our urgent care sinusitis visits, clinicians keep telling me families are calling back about diarrhea, yeast rash, and meds getting changed after a day or two, but the failure rate on the report looks flat across drugs. If the numbers don't reflect the callbacks, reassessments, and switched antibiotics we actually manage, frontline clinicians are going to stop trusting the stewardship message.
turns.utterance: I'm having trouble reconciling the first month of the sinusitis dashboard. The sites still leaning more on amoxicillin-clavulanate aren't showing a higher failure rate, but my teams are definitely hearing more diarrhea-related callbacks. So right now the story feels confusing.

turns.inner_thought: The aggregate report did what it was supposed to do. Across the full outpatient sinusitis denominator, treatment failure is low and the difference between amoxicillin and clavulanate isn't dramatic, which is actually pretty close to the published cohort. I need to keep us from chasing anecdote-driven metric changes that would undermine comparability or the build.
turns.utterance: Looking at the latest report, across our sinusitis cases the treatment failure rate stayed low overall and looked pretty similar between the two drugs. At a high level, that's not far off from what the published study showed.

turns.inner_thought: If failure really isn't separating them, then the practical issue is still urgent care prescribing behavior. Most routine sinusitis visits my clinicians see are uncomplicated sinusitis, aside from the obvious exceptions, and those are exactly the families calling back with side effects. I need a simple explanation I can give clinicians, not a lot of hidden carve-outs.
turns.utterance: If failure is truly similar, then the bigger issue may just be that we're still using clavulanate too often for uncomplicated sinusitis. Those are the kids whose families seem to be reaching back out to us.

turns.inner_thought: The CDS already narrows the first-line recommendation for uncomplicated sinusitis using the existing exclusion logic. A fair number of visits that look routine to a clinician were intentionally kept out because of inherited flags from the stewardship build. I don't want the group to assume the dashboard ignored that logic.
turns.utterance: That's fair, although the CDS already tries to reserve amoxicillin for uncomplicated sinusitis, and some of those visits were intentionally left outside the narrower first-line recommendation. So part of this may be how that group is being defined in the current build.

turns.inner_thought: We need chart review, not just one more aggregate graph. I want to look at last month's urgent care failures and see what actually happened: Did symptoms worsen, did someone switch the antibiotic, did the family call or message, did they need reassessment? Also, when we review same-day prescriptions, I mean what the clinician decided and sent at the visit, because that's what staff experience as prescribing.
turns.utterance: Why don't we pull a chart sample of last month's failures? I'd like to see, case by case, whether families got worse, switched antibiotics, or re-contacted the clinic after the initial prescription. Reviewing the same-day prescriptions against that might help us line this up with the study.

turns.inner_thought: That works if we anchor it to the analytic cohort. I'll start with children who had a same-day dispensed antibiotic, then see whether they had a downstream qualifying event in the 14-day window: new antibiotic fill, ED use, hospitalization. That's the study-style failure definition and keeps exposure certainty intact.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. I can start with children who had a same-day prescription and then look across the 14-day window for the downstream events we've been using for treatment failure.

turns.inner_thought: I especially don't want to lose the evening telehealth and urgent care workflows. Families often leave with a plan, the antibiotic is sent, and they pick it up the next morning. Clinically that's still the index prescribing decision. Those cases are common in urgent care-adjacent flow and matter for how the team interprets the report.
turns.utterance: One group I'd especially want included is the evening telehealth-to-urgent-care handoffs, where the antibiotic was chosen at the visit but the family may not have picked it up until the next morning. Those come up a lot in practice.

turns.inner_thought: If those next-morning pickups fall out under the same-day fill logic, we'll still have enough volume from the network-wide outpatient denominator. And the dashboard already includes urgent care, primary care, and telehealth, so it should capture the broader follow-up patterns. I don't think we need to re-scope to one service line unless the chart review really forces that.
turns.utterance: That should still leave us with plenty to review. The dashboard denominator already captures the relevant outpatient sinusitis encounters network-wide, including the follow-up patterns we've been monitoring, so we should be able to see whether the signal holds up.

turns.inner_thought: The broad numbers may be washing out what's happening in urgent care, where the prescribing push actually landed. If the aggregate network view is too smooth, I still need to understand why urgent care uncomplicated sinusitis isn't moving more toward amoxicillin. That's the conversation I have to have with site leads.
turns.utterance: If the broad numbers are masking the issue, then we may need to troubleshoot more specifically why uncomplicated sinusitis in urgent care isn't moving more strongly toward amoxicillin.

turns.inner_thought: Before we adjust the message to clinicians, I want to know how many urgent care sinusitis encounters were never in the uncomplicated group because of built-in exception flags in the current logic. Otherwise we'll be telling clinicians they overused clavulanate when the dashboard had already carved many of those cases out.
turns.utterance: I agree we should look there, but before changing the clinician messaging I want to verify whether a sizable share of those urgent care cases had built-in exception flags that kept them out of the uncomplicated group in the current logic.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I need something usable quickly. If we can review last month's failures and the adverse-event cases together, we can decide whether urgent care really has a prescribing behavior problem or whether the report is just not counting the events clinicians care about. I need to protect credibility with frontline staff before they write this off.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Can we do a quick review of last month's failures and the adverse-event cases, then decide whether we're looking at a real prescribing-behavior issue or just a reporting issue in how events are being counted?

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep this anchored to the current infrastructure: same-day fill logic, study-style failure definition, and flagged cases from the existing dashboard. Then we can chart check and see whether the perceived mismatch is due to clinical anecdotes versus measure construction. That lets me preserve reporting credibility while still responding to Elena's concern.
turns.utterance: Yes. I'll send a flagged-case list based on the current same-day prescription logic and the current treatment failure definition, and then we can reconvene after a chart-level check.
